title: Dual-Trigger of Series Nanowire Detector for Event-Based Photon Number Assignment
authors: Stefanie Grotowski, Daniel Landes, Fabian Wietschorke, Paul Pucknus, Rasmus Flaschmann, Torsten Langer, Torsten Krause, Kai Müller, Jonathan J. Finley
abstract: Photon-number-resolving (PNR) detectors are essential components of photonic quantum technologies. However, conventional single-channel edge-triggered readout struggles to resolve the photon number $n$ in real time or to characterize how timing jitter depends on $n$. In this work, we use a dual-trigger method on a three-pixel series-connected superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD) that triggers on both the rising and falling edges of the detection pulse. By doing so, we preserve the precise arrival time of the detection event while mapping the photon number onto the time interval between the rising and falling edges, allowing clear separation of the events. Using this technique, we assign each detection event to $n = 1, 2,$ or 3 photons with $99\,\%$ posterior confidence across all three classes. The timing jitter decreases as $n$ increases, reaching values below $41\, \text{ps}$ for $n \geq 2$. Comparing edge-triggering with constant-fraction discrimination (CFD) for arrival-time extraction, we find that CFD yields lower jitter for single-photon events and a nearly constant mean arrival time. Altogether, our results establish dual-triggering as a robust, low-latency readout scheme for PNR detectors, while revealing a photon-number dependence of the timing jitter relevant to timing precision achievable in heralded photonic quantum applications.
summary: This paper introduces a dual-trigger readout technique for superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors to overcome limitations in photon-number resolution. By measuring the time difference between the pulse's rising and falling edges, the authors can reliably assign the number of incident photons ($n=1, 2, 3$). The technique proves robust, offering high certainty and revealing that the timing jitter itself depends on the photon number, which is crucial for timing-sensitive quantum applications.
main_problem: Conventional single-channel readout methods struggle to resolve the photon number ($n$) in real time or accurately characterize how timing jitter depends on $n$ for photonic quantum technologies.
main_result: The dual-trigger method successfully establishes a robust, low-latency readout scheme, allowing for clear separation and assignment of $n=1, 2,$ or $3$ photons with high confidence.
method: The authors employ a dual-trigger method on a series-connected superconducting nanowire detector, triggering on both the rising and falling edges of the detection pulse to encode photon number in the time delay between these edges.
model_or_system: The experiment uses a three-pixel series-connected superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SND) operated at 2.3 K, read out using both edge-triggering and Constant-Fraction Discrimination (CFD) techniques.
key_observables: Photon number assignment ($n=1, 2, 3$), timing jitter (which decreases as $n$ increases), and the time interval ($\Delta t$) between the rising and falling edges.
important_parameters: The technique achieves 99% assignment certainty; timing jitter reaches values below 41 ps for $n \geq 2$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the time delay between the rising and falling edges can be reliably mapped to the photon number, and that CFD provides a superior, threshold-independent timestamp.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the waveform schematic showing separation via dual triggers, the measurement setup, and plots detailing timing jitter vs. photon number and mean arrival time shifts.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the limitations of current PNR detection, details the dual-trigger methodology using the SND, compares CFD vs. edge-triggering, presents quantitative results on photon number assignment certainty, and concludes by summarizing the photon-number-dependent jitter.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware limitations in quantum optics by providing a high-precision, low-latency readout mechanism essential for building quantum communication and computation devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Waveform schematic of how the trigger levels of the rising and falling edge are chosen to achieve separation in the 2D heatmap of the photon number.

FIG. 2: Schematic overview of used the measurement setup. The excitation light is guided to the SNSPDs through a pulse shaper, an AOM and VOA to control the pulse duration, repetition rate and attenuation, respectively. The SNSPD output signal is split into four channels, with three connected to the PicoHarp and one serving as a reference on the oscilloscope. The signal at channel (ii) is amplified and inverted to be compatible with the CFD mode.

FIG. 3: 2D heatmap of the delay of the rising edge and falling edge relative to the sync signal. a) CFD mode and b) Edge mode on rising edge. A clear separation of the photon levels in island shapes is visible.
